overview: This week's memory papers share a theme of questioning single-mechanism explanations. [Evidence that chunking works by building learned structure into the working memory representation](#p0), rather than by retrieving a stored average from long-term memory, sits alongside [experiments suggesting memory strength, not serial scanning, drives set-size costs in hybrid search](#p1), where fans searched better for 16 familiar logos than for 12 unfamiliar ones. [A study of true and false memories](#p3) found differences in spatiotemporal context memory, though they weren't fixed, and [an opinion piece on transient forgetting](#p5) surveys six kinds

papers.title: Chunking improves working memory via compression, not direct retrieval from long-term memory
papers.authors: Juan Manuel Chau Delgado, Joel Shebioba, Anna Pitt et al.
papers.summary: Chunking lets people remember far more than working memory's limit would suggest, but why is still debated. The researchers had people recall colour pairs whose hues varied slightly from trial to trial. Recall was still sensitive to the exact hue on each trial, so people weren't just pulling a stored average from long-term memory, yet responses were pulled toward each item's long-run mean, especially for chunkable pairs. A compression model fit best, and since mid-delay cues improved accuracy without reducing the bias, it seems the learned structure gets built into the working memory representation early on.
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) capacity is severely limited. Chunking, the process of grouping related items in WM, circumvents this limit and drastically improves performance. Despite decades of research, the mechanism underlying this benefit remains debated. One account proposes that statistical regularities allow multiple items to be compressed into structured WM representations, whereas another argues that structured associations are stored in long‑term memory (LTM) and reinstated at recall, effectively offloading storage demands. These accounts imply fundamentally different interactions between WM and long-term knowledge, yet in most paradigms, they make indistinguishable behavioural predictions. Here, we dissociate them by introducing small, continuous trial‑to‑trial variations in the hues of learned colour pairs, allowing us to test whether chunking benefits arise from compressed memory for the current hue (WM) or retrieval of long‑run feature means (LTM). Across two delayed colour report experiments, chunking reliably improved recall relative to unchunkable arrays. Participants remained sensitive to trial‑specific feature variations, indicating that responses were not driven by retrieval of feature means from LTM templates. At the same time, responses were systematically biased toward each item’s long‑run mean, especially on chunkable trials. To explain this bias, we fit psychophysical models derived from the competing compression and LTM‑retrieval accounts. The compression-based model, in which compression produces graded biases toward learned means within WM, outperformed the LTM-retrieval and baseline models. In a second experiment, we examined whether these biases arise during encoding/maintenance or at the recall stage. Cues in the maintenance period indicating which item would be probed improved recall accuracy but did not reduce bias toward learned structure, indicating that the bias arose during encoding or early maintenance rather than retrieval. These findings show that chunking enhances WM by integrating learned structure into WM representations through compression, rather than by offloading to LTM.

papers.title: Memory strength drives hybrid search efficiency
papers.authors: Dyllan Simpson, Lauren Williams, Haven Vander Bie et al.
papers.summary: The usual story for why hybrid search slows as you memorize more targets is a serial scan through memory. These experiments suggest memory strength may be the real driver. Strengthening memories through repetition and deeper encoding improved search at the same set size, and NFL and NHL fans searched better for 16 familiar team logos than for 12 unfamiliar ones, reversing the typical set-size effect. A standard recognition-memory model (REM), fit only to memory data, reproduced the pattern, so set-size costs may not reflect serial scanning at all.
papers.abstract: In hybrid search tasks, observers search for any of multiple targets held in memory (e.g., finding all of the ingredients for a recipe in the supermarket). Performance declines with the log of the number of memorized targets, a cost often attributed to a serial scan through memory. In standard models of recognition memory, however, holding more items in memory weakens the match strength between each memory representation and the corresponding visual item – independent of any serial search process. Here we propose an account of hybrid search based on memory strength, testing how memory strength affects hybrid search separately from memory set size. We found that strengthening memories through repetition and deeper encoding improved hybrid search at matched set sizes (Exp. 1). Taking advantage of NFL and NHL fans' pre-existing memory strength for sports logos (Exps. 2–3), we next found search was better for a larger set of familiar items (16 logos) than for a smaller set of unfamiliar items (12 logos), a reversal of the usual memory set-size effect. A standard global matching model (REM), with encoding parameters fit only to memory performance, not search data, reproduced these results and the canonical, approximately log-linear set-size cost in discriminability. Memory strength is thus a potentially strong determinant of hybrid search efficiency, with set-size effects not necessarily reflecting any serial memory search. Instead, models of recognition memory may provide a productive framework for the memory component of hybrid search.

papers.title: When looking away means looking inward: contextual interpretation of gaze aversions determines their attentional value
papers.authors: Amit Zehngut, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg
papers.summary: When someone looks away while thinking hard, should you follow their gaze? Across two pre-registered experiments, people did a gaze-cueing letter task with identical gaze shifts, but one group was told to see them as the person thinking effortfully. That group showed noticeably weaker attentional orienting toward the gaze direction. It's a neat demonstration that gaze following depends on what we infer the other person's eye movement means, not just on the movement itself.
papers.abstract: Eye movements are typically understood as supporting outward orienting, directing attention toward locations of interest in the external environment. However, not all eye movements reflect outward orienting. Gaze aversions, the common tendency to look away during effortful cognitive processing, serve as social signals of inward-oriented attention and ongoing processing. Because observers continuously monitor others' eye movements and use gaze-related cues to guide their own behavior, distinguishing between outward-oriented gaze-shifts and inward-oriented gaze aversions is a basic challenge in human interaction. Here, we examine the hypothesis that this distinction depends on the context in which gaze shifts appear. While participants reorient their attention following an outward-oriented gaze shift, they withhold doing so when the context suggests that the gaze shift reflects inward-oriented processing. To test this hypothesis, we relied on the Gaze Cueing Effect (GCE), an attentional orienting to observed gaze shifts that is known to be modulated by top-down context and interpretation. In two pre-registered experiments (total N = 90), participants performed a gaze-cueing letter-discrimination task while viewing identical gaze shifts within different contexts. One group was led to interpret the gaze shifts as occurring during effortful thinking, whereas the other group received no thinking-related context. Across both experiments, attentional orienting was significantly reduced when gaze shifts were perceived as reflecting internal cognitive processing rather than attention shifts. These findings demonstrate that gaze aversions function as communicative signals that dynamically regulate interpersonal attention, and that gaze following depends fundamentally on the inferred social meaning of the observed eye movement.

papers.title: Probing spatiotemporal context reveals differences between true and false memories
papers.authors: Brynn E. Sherman
papers.summary: Do false memories look any different from true ones? Using the Deese-Roediger-McDermott word-list paradigm, the researchers asked people about the when and where of what they remembered. Context memory was more consistent, and confidence in it differed, for true versus false memories, even after controlling for confidence that the item had been seen at all. The differences weren't fixed, though, since in some circumstances false memories seemed to carry genuine context traces.
papers.abstract: Our memories do not faithfully represent the past, but rather are reconstructive, rendering them susceptible to the intrusion of false memories. However, the nature of the false memories is debated: Do false memories reflect the retrieval of a genuine, erroneous memory trace, or are they the product of semantic associations? This question reflects the fact that although some findings suggest that false memories can be phenomenologically compelling and rich in details, others suggest that there are subtle cues that distinguish true and false memories. Here, we take a novel approach to this question by assessing memory for the spatiotemporal context of false memories - the when and where of those memories. We demonstrate that context memory can provide a probabilistic cue to whether a memory is true or false in the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm. Across participants, the reliability of reported context memory (i.e., the consistency with which people report remembering when or where a false memory occurred) revealed differences between true and false memories. Additionally, confidence in memory for context (both within and across participants) differed between true and false memories - even when controlling for confidence in having encountered the false memory. However, these effects were malleable: Under certain circumstances, false memories appeared to have genuine context traces. Together, these data provide new insights into the circumstances under which true and false memories differ in subtle but meaningful ways, speaking to theories of how false memories may arise from the reconstructive nature of memory.

papers.title: Conflict between representational formats and procedures constrains visual tracking
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum
papers.summary: Does vision group scene elements into a shape and track them relative to that whole, like grouping objects in PowerPoint? In seven pre-registered tracking experiments, people followed a target among identical items arranged into geometric shapes. Tracking was good when the shapes rotated, which fits a shape-centred representation, but worse when items moved independently in translation, as if the representation and the task were mismatched. The effect held across occluded, rounded and irregular shapes and shrank when the cues that create structure were disrupted.
papers.abstract: Computer-assisted design software, such as PowerPoint, groups separate elements to create structured objects whose parts can be manipulated relative to the whole. Might visual perception perform a similar operation, grouping scene elements and representing them with internal reference to the emergent structure? The proposal is central yet perennially controversial in cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind. In a series of seven preregistered tracking experiments, we identify internally referenced representations in human vision by relying on the logic that, as in computer-assisted design, a representation will make certain procedures easy to access while limiting others. Participants tracked a target among identical nontargets organized into geometric shapes. When the shapes rotated, performance was high, suggesting the use of internally referenced, shape-centered representations that naturally support rotational transformations. In contrast, performance declined in translation conditions, where constituent items moved independently, revealing a mismatch between the internally structured representation and the requisite, externally oriented tracking procedure. This effect replicated across diverse stimuli, including occluded, rounded, and irregular shapes, and was reduced when structure-inducing cues were disrupted. These findings identify representational format and its compatibility with task procedures as an important determinant of visual performance.

papers.title: Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
papers.authors: Milan Van Maldegem, Hans Op de Beeck, Niels A. Taatgen et al.
papers.summary: Neural networks sometimes show a 'stability gap', where a network that already learned one task temporarily forgets it when training on a second task begins. This opinion piece asks whether humans do something similar. A literature survey turned up six kinds of transient forgetting in people (from learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching and multitasking), all different from the stability gap but possibly sharing some mechanisms. It closes by proposing experiments to look for a stability-gap-like effect in humans.
papers.abstract: Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a 'stability gap-like' form of TF also occurs in humans.

papers.title: The second-language word age of acquisition effect and its relation to first-language word age of acquisition: Evidence from multitask megastudies.
papers.authors: Xue Zhang, Jue Wang, Lu Jiao et al.
papers.summary: Words learned earlier in life are processed faster, and this study asked how that age-of-acquisition effect works in a second language and whether it depends on when the first-language translation was learned. Four experiments, three of them megastudies, covered orthographic, phonological and semantic processing. The L2 effect was independent of L1 age of acquisition for spelling, sound and shallow meaning tasks, but in deeper semantic processing it appeared only when the L1 translation was learned early. The authors propose an 'independence-dependence dual-path' model to explain this.
papers.abstract: Megastudies were used in the present research in order to systematically explore the age of acquisition (AoA) effect in second-language (L2) lexical processing and its relationship with the AoA of the corresponding first-language (L1) translation equivalents. To capture different levels of processing, we conducted three experiments using large-scale lexical stimuli: a letter search task for orthographic processing (Experiment 1), a lexical naming task for phonological processing (Experiment 2), and a personal name judgment task for semantic processing (Experiment 3). As a critical supplement to those megastudies, Experiment 4 employed a more typical semantic categorization task (living or nonliving semantic judgment) to induce deeper semantic engagement. The results showed that the L2 AoA effect was reliable and independent of L1 AoA at the orthographic and phonological levels. This pattern further extended to shallow semantic processing, where the L2 AoA effect remained evident regardless of L1 AoA. However, at deeper levels of semantic processing, the effect was modulated by L1 AoA: The L2 AoA effect appeared only when the L1 translation equivalent was acquired early. We propose a theoretical framework, the independence-dependence dual-path model, to help account for the L2 AoA effect. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Metacognition and meta-metacognition for common perceptual experiences.
papers.authors: Yi Gao, Herrick Fung, Dobromir Rahnev
papers.summary: How well do people understand their own everyday perception, and how well do they know when they're right? Participants answered a 43-item questionnaire about common perceptual experiences and rated their confidence in each answer. Overall they showed both kinds of insight, but six questions produced below-chance accuracy, and confidence tracked accuracy poorly for those. Confidence followed performance closely only for topics people understood well, so the limits of this self-knowledge show up in the harder domains.
papers.abstract: = 200) completed a 43-item questionnaire covering common perceptual experiences and indicated their confidence in each response. We defined accurate beliefs about one's perception as evidence of metacognition, and confidence that distinguishes true from false beliefs as evidence of meta-metacognition. Overall, participants exhibited both metacognitive insight and meta-metacognitive ability to evaluate their own insight. However, six questions produced below-chance accuracy, indicating poor metacognition. These questions also exhibited chance-level or below-chance-level confidence-accuracy correlation, indicating poor meta-metacognition. Furthermore, confidence-accuracy correlation was at chance for over half of the questions, including many with above-chance accuracy. Finally, average confidence stayed roughly constant for the questions with poor-to-average accuracy, but closely followed performance for questions with above-average accuracy. These results reveal that people show excellent meta-metacognition for aspects of perception they understand well, but poor meta-metacognition for more challenging domains. Our results begin to reveal the limits of people's metacognitive and meta-metacognitive beliefs about their everyday perception. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Older adults retain detail-specific associations: Evidence from an indirect memory test
papers.authors: Anna K. Lawrance, Tarek Amer
papers.summary: Older adults often struggle with episodic memory, which has been linked to trouble forming detailed associations. Using an indirect test with scene-object pairs, where response times reveal memory without asking for recall, the researchers found that older adults did form detail-specific associations, though only with longer encoding time. In a second experiment, the response-time effects replicated, even though older adults did worse than younger adults on a standard recognition test. So the associations seem to be there and can be accessed when retrieval demands are low.
papers.abstract: Research suggests that age-related episodic memory decline is characterized by a reduced ability to form detailed associations. In two experiments, we test this claim using a sensitive, indirect memory test and additionally examine how associative encoding is influenced by encoding duration. In Experiment 1, young and older adult participants studied scene-object pairs for varying durations before completing a speeded congruency judgment task involving intact, recombined, and new pairs. Recombined pairs varied based on detail-specific, perceptual (related pairs), or conceptual (unrelated pairs) features. Participants in both age groups were generally slower to respond to recombined than intact pairs on the congruency judgment task. Critically, both groups formed detail-specific associations, as evidenced by slower response times to related compared to intact pairs - though this effect emerged only at longer encoding durations for older adults. In Experiment 2, using a similar paradigm, we replicated the response time effects in older adults using a single encoding duration and additionally observed poorer memory for recombined pairs relative to young adults on a traditional recognition (direct) memory task. Our findings indicate that older adults can form detailed associations, as demonstrated by faster response times to intact compared to recombined pairs, and can access those associations when retrieval demands are minimized in indirect memory tests.

papers.title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
papers.authors: Jirko Rubruck, Alice Zhang, Andrew Saxe et al.
papers.summary: Learning simple rules before exceptions helps people, and this work offers a computational explanation using both human behaviour and neural networks. Both kinds of learner showed a simplicity bias, settling on simple rules that underfit the data, and in networks this came with compressed internal representations. Simple-to-complex curricula helped learners get past that compression, and the theory's prediction held that learners with more compressed starting representations benefited more. In effect, curricula seem to help with 'unlearning' the simple rules.
papers.abstract: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

papers.title: The Impact of Social Learning on Learning Traps
papers.authors: Yanjun Liu, Alisha Shaikh, Ben R Newell et al.
papers.summary: A learning trap happens when a false belief about how the world is structured leads you to under-explore rewarding options. Across five studies (N = 1342), watching another learner's decisions helped many trapped participants shift to the optimal two-dimensional rule, even when the other learner used a suboptimal rule. When observation came before private learning, though, it reduced traps if the demonstrator modelled the optimal rule and increased them if the demonstrator used a one-dimensional rule. Social learning can therefore get people out of traps, but poorly coordinated social learning can deepen them.
papers.abstract: People often fall into learning traps where a false belief about the structure of the environment leads to under-exploration of rewarding options. Five studies (N = 1342) examined whether observation of decisions made by another learner facilitated escape from a trap or increased trap prevalence. In studies of horizontal social learning (Experiments 1a, 1b, 2), participants first had private experience with a task where approach of different category members could lead to gains or losses. We identified whether participants had learned an optimal two-dimensional categorization rule or fallen into the trap of using a one-dimensional rule. Participants then observed the approach decisions of another learner using the same or a different category rule. A substantial proportion of those who had initially fallen into the trap shifted to the optimal rule after observing use of an alternate rule. This escape from a learning trap was found following observation of both optimal (Experiment 1a) and sub-optimal rules (Experiment 1b, 2). In vertical social learning (Experiments 3, 4), social observation of approach decisions took place before private learning. Such observation led to reduced trap prevalence when the social demonstrator modeled an optimal rule but increased trap prevalence when they modeled a one-dimensional rule. These effects generalized to a learning environment with the same underlying feature structure but different feature-category mappings. These results both offer a novel approach to remediating learning traps as well as highlighting how poorly coordinated social learning can intensify traps.

papers.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
papers.authors: Bianca de Haan
papers.summary: When your mind wanders, does perception dim everywhere or mainly on one side of space? In a pre-registered online signal detection task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering. Sensitivity (d′) was lower on mind-wandering trials, as the decoupling hypothesis predicts, but the drop was the same for stimuli in the left and right visual fields. That points to a global reduction in sensory processing rather than a lateralised one.
papers.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

papers.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
papers.authors: Esther Boissin, Thomas H Costello, David Gertler Rand et al.
papers.summary: Which beliefs can a chatbot talk people out of? Over 3,000 online U.S. adults discussed a conspiracy or other suspect belief with GPT-4, which was instructed to debunk it with facts. Confidence dropped in every domain, but how much it dropped depended on the belief's evidential status rather than its topic. Beliefs open to counterevidence (strongly, weakly or un-investigated) changed a lot, while non-falsifiable and well-supported beliefs changed little.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

papers.title: Seeing Events in 3D Enhances Scene Memory and Vividness
papers.authors: Peggy L. St. Jacques, Júlia Feminella Duarte da Costa, Shikang Peng
papers.summary: Most memory experiments use flat 2D stimuli, so the researchers tested whether binocular depth changes how events are remembered. Participants watched first-person 360° videos in VR, either monoscopic (2D) or stereoscopic (3D), with everything else held constant. Events seen in 3D were later rated as having stronger scene-related qualities and more vividness, and this wasn't explained by how present people felt. Emotional intensity and pleasantness were unaffected, so depth seems to shape the spatial and visual side of remembering in particular.
papers.abstract: Episodic memories arise from perceptually rich, spatially structured experiences, yet most laboratory studies rely on two-dimensional (2D) stimuli that omit key features of naturalistic perception. We tested whether one such feature—binocular depth—alters how events are later remembered. Participants viewed immersive, first-person 360° videos presented in either 2D (monoscopic) or 3D (stereoscopic) virtual reality while the display, field of view, and context were held constant. Events experienced in 3D were rated as having stronger scene-related qualities and greater vividness than events experienced in 2D. These differences remained after accounting for both within-person and between-person variation in subjective presence, indicating that presence alone did not explain the effects of depth. Depth did not systematically alter emotional intensity or pleasantness. These findings show that binocular depth selectively influences the spatial and visual qualities of later remembering and that conventional 2D presentation may omit perceptual information that shapes how episodic memories are formed.

papers.title: People make history-dependent decisions in Markovian environments
papers.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi, Evan Russek, Ionatan Kuperwajs et al.
papers.summary: Researchers looked at 74,304 online chess players, zeroing in on 183,775 cases where the same player met the same board position in two different games. Since a chess position contains everything needed to pick the best move, how the game got there shouldn't matter, yet players' choices were still biased by the history of the current game. Even highly trained, motivated people seem to be swayed by contextual traces rather than relying purely on the abstract state.
papers.abstract: Many real-world decisions are history-dependent, such that the appropriate action depends on recent events. However, people may also encounter history-independent environments, where all information relevant for action selection is contained in the current state. Here, we tested whether people can adapt to such environments by analyzing the behavior of 74,304 online chess players, focusing on 183,775 instances where a player encountered the same board position in two different games. In chess, the configuration of pieces on the board fully specifies the information relevant for optimal play, making the history of the current game redundant. Nevertheless, we find that players’ behavior is biased to be history-dependent. Our findings challenge assumptions about humans’ ability to decide based on a task’s abstract state representation, instead suggesting that contextual traces play a significant role in biasing behavior even when individuals are highly trained and motivated to perform at their best.

papers.title: Semantigories: A large-scale investigation of form-meaning interactions and category-level differences in semantic memory search
papers.authors: Abhilasha Ashok Kumar, Channing Everidge Hambric, Larry Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Using verbal fluency data from 1,245 people across six categories (Animals, Occupations, Things at the Beach, and more), this work treats memory search as a trade-off between exploring and exploiting, guided by meaning, sound, and word frequency. Searching for animals fit a strategic foraging pattern, while looser categories like Excuses for Being Late led to more idiosyncratic search with short hops between similar, easily accessible items. People who made good use of form-meaning links in structured and functional categories did better, and the dataset is openly available for others.
papers.abstract: Humans routinely search for information within their mental lexicon, and this process involves navigating across clusters of related items within a complex lexical landscape. However, concepts can be related in several ways, and prior work has examined semantic memory search primarily within taxonomic categories (e.g., Animals) and underemphasized interactions between lexical sources that guide search and retrieval. The present work examined memory search via the verbal fluency task across different semantic categories as an explore-exploit trade-off mediated by semantic, phonological, and frequency-based information within the lexicon. This account was tested on a large-scale compilation of semantic fluency data (N=1245) across six diverse categorical domains (Animals, Occupations, Things at the Beach, Things in a Classroom, Things to Rescue from a Burning Home and Excuses for Being Late), being made openly available for future research via https://semantigories.research.bowdoin.edu/. Search behavior was consistent with a strategic foraging account within the taxonomic category Animals, whereas search in categories with less rigid organization was relatively impaired, highly idiosyncratic, and relied more on short-range transitions indicating a strong tendency to select the most similar and accessible items. Fluency performance was enhanced for individuals who adequately leveraged form-meaning mappings within structured and functional categories, suggesting that memory search involves both automatic and strategic components. The present results thus highlight the flexibility of both semantic representations and search processes in human cognition.

papers.title: The Problem of Common False-Alarm Rates and the Informational Asymmetry When Comparing Pure and Mixed Lists in Recognition Memory: Reconsidering the List-Strength Effect
papers.authors: Raz Danino, Yonatan Goshen-Gottstein
papers.summary: The list-strength effect asks whether strengthening some items hurts memory for others differently in pure versus mixed lists, and it has been used to test recognition models. This paper argues that the usual comparison is flawed, because mixed lists force a common false-alarm rate while pure lists let it vary, so sensitivity estimates aren't built from equivalent parts. A hypothetical reanalysis shows plausible false-alarm changes could yield list-strength effects in any direction, leading the authors to conclude that pure-mixed comparisons can't decide between recognition theories.
papers.abstract: The list-strength effect (LSE)—the interaction between item strength and list composition (pure versus mixed)—is theoretically diagnostic in models of memory. In contrast to free recall, in old-new recognition, the LSE was long considered negligible. This dissociation prompted the development of new recognition models. Recent work, however, suggests that the magnitude and direction of the LSE depend on the strength manipulation. Here, we argue that conclusions about the LSE are undermined by two methodological limitations in pure-mixed comparisons: a design flaw and an informational asymmetry. Sensitivity measures in recognition memory depend jointly on hit and false-alarm rates (HRs and FARs), which co-vary when sensitivity, response bias, or both change. When strength conditions differ only for studied items, sensitivity estimates from pure and mixed lists are not constructed from equivalent components. This is because traditional mixed-list designs, which impose a common FAR across strength conditions, are compared to pure lists wherein FARs can vary freely. Critically, there is no contingency in which given differences in HRs, a common FAR of any magnitude would lead researchers to attribute those differences to bias rather than to sensitivity—regardless of which sensitivity measure is used. We consider two possible arguments in favor of common FARs and refute both. Using a hypothetical reanalysis of recent LSE data, we show that empirically plausible changes in FAR—without altering observed HRs—can produce LSEs of any direction. We conclude that pure-mixed comparisons cannot adjudicate between theories of recognition memory. Alternative experimental designs are then discussed.

papers.title: Toward a Formal Theory of Cognitive Effort: Application of Linear Control Theory to a Simple Cognitive Model of Controlled Processing
papers.authors: Clay B. Holroyd
papers.summary: Linear control theory, an engineering framework for steering dynamical systems, has been proposed as a way to think about cognitive effort as the energy needed to hold the brain in states away from its natural dynamics. Here the idea is applied for the first time to a classic neurocomputational model of cognitive control. It's a proof-of-concept that links the control-theory view to existing models, with discussion of how it relates to other effort theories and how it could be tested.
papers.abstract: Cognitive effort is a defining feature of cognitive control but theories about its origin and purpose have long been controversial. Recently, it has been proposed that cognitive effort can be understood using linear control theory, a mathematical formalism developed in the engineering literature to control dynamical systems. On this view, effort levels reflect the energy required by the cognitive control system to support representational states that deviate from the intrinsic dynamics of the cognitive system. Although this approach has been used to characterize the energy landscape of neural networks abstracted from the human structural and functional connectome, it has yet to make contact with neurocomputational models of cognitive control. Here we demonstrate the potential of this approach by applying LCT to a classic computational model of cognitive control, and discuss its broader significance in the context of other models of cognitive effort and future studies that can test the theory.

papers.title: The context-dependent evolution of structure learning and metacognition
papers.authors: Rochelle Kaper, Megan A. K. Peters
papers.summary: Participants learned a two-level probabilistic structure, with stimulus pairings embedded in a sequence, using either unfamiliar fractals or familiar line drawings, and no feedback. Learning and confidence followed different paths depending on the stimuli: fractals showed sequence learning ahead of pair learning while line drawings showed the reverse, and metacognitive sensitivity grew across cycles for fractals but stayed flat for line drawings even as accuracy improved. So learning and self-evaluation seem to depend heavily on context and complexity rather than generalizing neatly.
papers.abstract: Humans learn multiple probabilistic regularities at once, and often without feedback, which may be aided by metacognitive evaluations throughout learning. To understand this learning-metacognition relationship, we must first characterize how both capacities co-evolve as environmental structures are internalized, especially when feedback is unavailable. Here, participants learned a two-level probabilistic environment in which stimulus co-occurrences were embedded within a sequence, using unfamiliar fractals and familiar line drawings in a two-session, within-subjects design (N=63; N=50 completed both sessions). For each stimulus set, we measured learning across six repeating exposure-test cycles, using a cover task during exposure phases and forced-choice questions in test phases; test questions also included confidence judgments. Results revealed stimulus- and structure-dependent learning and metacognitive signatures. First, learning dynamics differed across stimuli: fractal sequence test accuracy outpaced co-occurrence accuracy, but vice versa for line drawings. Further, confidence increased across blocks, and was higher for line drawings as well as co-occurrences and first but not second sequence selections. Finally, both metacognitive sensitivity and test accuracy increased in successive exposure-test cycles for fractals, but metacognitive sensitivity remained stagnant for line drawings even as test accuracy improved. These results demonstrate that structure learning and metacognitive processes are highly context- and complexity-dependent rather than being completely generalizable. This study informs future directions for refining theories of learning without feedback, including how people evaluate their own learning and uncertainty and the interaction of both cognitive abilities with task design, stimuli, and environmental structures.

papers.title: Environmental regularities shape visual search strategy selection
papers.authors: Chris Ahn, Wouter Kool
papers.summary: In a visual search task, targets appeared in one of two color-defined groups whose relative sizes varied, so searching the smaller (more salient) group is a bottom-up strategy and favoring the larger group takes top-down control. By changing where targets were likely to be, the researchers made different strategies pay off, and people adapted, but unevenly. They readily leaned on salient minority groups when it helped, yet only prioritized the majority group when salience cues were minimized, suggesting that overriding salience carries a real cognitive cost.
papers.abstract: Visual search can be guided by multiple strategies, some of them relying on bottom-up salience, others on top-down expectations. However, little is known about how we arbitrate between these strategies. Here, we tested whether environmental regularities that incentivize different strategies can influence this arbitration. Participants performed a visual search task in which targets appeared in one of two color-defined groups of items whose relative sizes varied across trials. Because smaller groups are more visually salient, prioritizing them constitutes a bottom-up search strategy, and prioritizing the larger group requires top-down control. By manipulating the probability that the target appeared in each group, we created environments in which abstract structural properties of the display (the relative size of the groups) incentivized different strategies. Participants adapted their search strategy to these abstract regularities, but in an asymmetric fashion. Reliance on salient minority groups readily increased when it was advantageous, whereas people only became willing to prioritize the majority group when alternative salience-based cues were minimized. These results suggest that visual search strategies are shaped by environmental statistics, but their adoption is constrained by the cognitive costs of overriding bottom-up salience.

papers.title: Simulation-Based Evidence Accumulation Modeling for Single- and Multi-Response Tasks: The eam Package
papers.authors: Guangyu Zhu, Guang Yang
papers.summary: Evidence accumulation models are great for single choices, but are hard to apply to tasks like free recall or verbal fluency where one trial has many responses, because the likelihoods are intractable. The authors built an R package, eam, that uses simulation-based inference and includes five models (diffusion decision, leaky competing accumulator, linear ballistic accumulator, racing diffusion, and Lévy flight) extended to multiple responses. Simulations showed parameters could be recovered well, and an application to an aging free-recall dataset showed it can reveal mechanisms behind age differences in retrieval.
papers.abstract: Evidence accumulation models are widely used to model choices and reaction times incognitive tasks. Despite their success in binary and multi-alternative decision-making, theirapplication to sequential multi-response tasks, such as free recall and verbal fluency, hasremained limited. The primary challenge in modeling multiple responses within a singletrial lies in the absence of tractable likelihood functions. To address this limitation, weintroduce simulation-based inference into the evidence accumulation framework anddevelop an R package that integrates simulation engines for five representative models (thediffusion decision model, leaky competing accumulator model, linear ballistic accumulatormodel, racing diffusion model, and Lévy flight model), extending them to themulti-response contexts. Across three simulation studies, the package demonstrated robustparameter recovery across representative models, their multi-response extensions, andcovariate-dependent variants. An empirical application to an aging-related free recalldataset further demonstrated the package’s ability to uncover computational mechanismsunderlying age-related differences in memory retrieval. Taken together, this packageprovides a foundation for building customized evidence accumulation models and expandsthe range of cognitive processes that can be studied within the evidence accumulationframework.

papers.title: The crossword effect: A recall advantage for words encoded in alignment with their spatial associations
papers.authors: Christoph Scheepers, Ricarda Senger
papers.summary: In two preregistered experiments, people recalled words better when they were presented in a direction matching the word's spatial association. Vertically associated words like 'rocket' were remembered better when shown vertically, but horizontally associated words like 'railway' got no such boost from horizontal presentation. Spatially neutral words also benefited from vertical presentation, which hints at a general vertical advantage and fits the idea that word meanings are grounded in perception and action.
papers.abstract: Across two preregistered experiments, we demonstrate that free word recall improves when words are encoded in alignment with their spatial associations. Experiment 1 compared words with a strong horizontal association (e.g., railway) to words with a strong vertical association (e.g., rocket) and established that the latter were more likely to be recalled when presented vertically rather than horizontally during encoding. No such benefit was observed for horizontally associated words. Experiment 2 extended these findings by showing a vertical encoding advantage also for spatially neutral words (e.g., foam), which was smaller than for the vertically associated words but larger than for the horizontally associated words in Experiment 1. Beyond suggesting a general vertical encoding advantage in free word recall, the results support Barsalou's (1999) Perceptual Symbol Hypothesis, which posits that word meanings are grounded in perception and action. Our findings demonstrate that access to word concepts in short term memory is modulated by sensorimotor processes during encoding, specifically horizontal versus vertical reading.

papers.title: Worse Directed Forgetting After a Repeated Attempt
papers.authors: Vinni Ott, Eric-Jan Wagenmakers, Jan Rummel
papers.summary: In a directed forgetting experiment with 120 participants, items were followed by a remember or forget cue, and some items were shown twice with the same cue. Repeating a forget item made it better remembered, to the point that twice-presented forget items were about as well recognized as once-presented remember items, so trying to forget a second time worked worse. Repetition also helped forget items less than remember items. Passive forgetting through selective rehearsal can explain this, though two active-forgetting accounts (inhibition and unbinding from context) remain compatible too.
papers.abstract: Intentional remembering and forgetting are both adaptive human abilities. The formerbenefits from a repeated attempt to remember. Yet, it is unclear how a repeated attemptto forget would affect intentional forgetting. In this item-method directed forgettingexperiment, 120 participants studied items one-by-one and after each item, a cue signaledto either remember it (R item) or to forget it (F item). Half of the items of both typeswere studied once (R1, F1) and the other half twice (R2, F2; spaced repetition while cuesremained constant across repetitions). In a subsequent old-new recognition test, itemmemory was better for R2 than for R1 items and weaker for F1 than for R1 items.Critically, memory was stronger for F2 than F1 items. This effect was remarkably large:memory for F2 items was about as strong as that for R1 items. Moreover, repetitionstrengthened memory for F2 items less than for R2 items. These results can be readilyexplained by passive forgetting as assumed by the selective rehearsal account of directedforgetting. However, the results are also compatible with two active-forgetting accounts,namely an inhibition of F items and an unbinding of F items from their context.

papers.title: The role of sequence stability on serial dependence
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
papers.summary: Serial dependence is the pull of recent stimuli on current perception, and it's usually strongest when consecutive stimuli look similar. Here, participants saw sequences of Gabor patches with similar orientations where spatial frequency was either constant or random. Serial dependence showed up consistently but was stronger in the random condition, which the authors link to predictive coding sharpening representations in stable settings so past information is needed less. They also saw a form of optimal integration of past and present when uncertainty about the final Gabor was low.
papers.abstract: Perception and decision-making are strongly influenced by previously presented information. Research on serial dependence has revealed significant attractive biases towards previous stimuli, suggesting that integrating information from both past and present stimuli is beneficial when representing information about the environment. Strong serial dependence is mainly found when consecutive stimuli are similar providing evidence that serial dependence supports continuity. Small changes in the stimulus are not perceived as meaningful stimulus changes and should hence be integrated. In the current study we examined the role of continuity further and presented sequences of Gabors which were similar in their orientation, but their spatial frequency was either constant or random. This created stable and unstable environments. We consistently found serial dependence. Interestingly, serial dependence was stronger when the spatial frequency was random compared to constant. In stable contexts, predictive coding mechanisms might sharpen neural representations of the expected input, improve discrimination and reduce the need to integrate past information.Additionally, a form of optimal integration was observed when the uncertainty of the final Gabor was low. Using similar orientations across longer sequences seemed to induce a form of optimal integration of past and present information, potentially creating the continuous perception of a single object when the current trial's uncertainty was low.

papers.title: A rational cascade from teaching explains strategy discovery in development: The case of early addition
papers.authors: Merrick Giles, Andrew Perfors, Francis Mollica
papers.summary: Children often discover faster, more accurate addition strategies without being taught them. This model proposes they get there by first imitating teaching, then doing rational inference under pressure for speed or accuracy, formalized as Bayesian program induction with a preference for algorithmic simplicity. Whether the pressure is for speed or accuracy, the model reproduces the long-observed developmental trajectory of strategy discovery, offering an alternative to accounts where children rewrite their own strategies metacognitively.
papers.abstract: Without being taught, children learning addition discover strategies that are faster and less error-prone than those in their repertoire. Leading explanations of strategy discovery propose metacognitive mechanisms where children iteratively rewrite their existing strategies. Departing from this tradition, we propose that children make discoveries through a combination of reconstructive imitation during teaching, followed by rational inference under basic performance pressures. We instantiate our proposal with a model of Bayesian program induction with a prior for algorithmic simplicity and a likelihood that first encodes a pressure of mimicry (teaching phase), and then a pressure for speed and/or accuracy (individual practice phase). Regardless of whether the pressure is to respond faster or more accurately, the model robustly captures the long-observed developmental trajectory of strategy discovery.

papers.title: Origin and Control of Persistent Mental Content
papers.authors: Gabriel Kressin Palacios, Tianshu Ouyang, Buddhika Bellana et al.
papers.summary: Using immersive narratives to induce thoughts that linger for minutes, the researchers found that this persistent content was spontaneous rather than just deliberate memory retrieval, and that it held up against several kinds of distractor tasks. When new information was seen as related to the earlier experience, that experience lingered longer. The authors suggest memory models need a slowly changing 'deep context' representation that resists interference and shapes both retrieval and the next thought.
papers.abstract: Some thoughts and experiences persist in our minds on the scale of minutes. For example, topics discussed earlier in a conversation remain fresh in mind and may persist in our thinking after the conversation is over. What cognitive mechanisms underlie this persistent mental content and how can it be controlled? To answer these questions, we induced persistent mental content using immersive narrative stimuli and measured the rate and influence of persistent thoughts.First, we found that persistent mental content was spontaneous and not merely a consequence of intentional memory retrieval. Second, we found that persistent content was robust to interference from multiple types of similar and dissimilar distractor tasks. Finally, we found that when new information was construed as related to the preceding experience, the persistence of the preceding experience was prolonged. These data indicate that memory models need to be augmented with a slowly changing "deep context" representation which is robust to stimulus-driven interference and which biases both retrieval and the generation of the next thought.

papers.title: Testing the Limits of Cumulative Semantic Interference in Word Production: Implications for Adaptive Models
papers.authors: Jörg D. Jescheniak, Stefan Wöhner
papers.summary: In continuous picture naming, each earlier word from the same category slows naming by a constant amount, an effect that motivates adaptive models of word production, though it had only been tested across five or six positions. Testing ten and fifteen positions, the researchers found the increase in interference was limited rather than continuing linearly, which conflicts with current adaptive models. Interference also dropped after a long lag with unrelated naming, and its build-up looked similar before and after the lag, so those models need adjusting.
papers.abstract: It was repeatedly found that when speakers produced a word, such as “lion”, they were slowed by a constant amount of time for each previously produced word from the same semantic category, for example the words “elephant” or “zebra”. That is, there was a linear relationship between the ordinal position of a category exemplar in the experimental list and the naming latency. This cumulative semantic interference effect observed in the context of the continuous picture naming task is the main motivation for adaptive models of word production. Notably, all studies reporting this effect have examined the interference only across five (or six in one case) ordinal positions. We investigated whether this linear increase continues when testing ten or fifteen ordinal positions. Inconsistent with the predictions of current adaptive models, but consistent with evidence from the learning literature, we found that the increase in the interference was restricted. Additionally, we found that the interference decreased with a long lag (introducing unrelated naming episodes) and that its developmental trajectory was similar before and after the lag. These findings require an adjustment to existing adaptive models of word production.

papers.title: Non-commitment in mental imagery is distinct from perceptual inattention, and supports hierarchical scene construction
papers.authors: Yichen Li, Veronika Hammond, Tomer David Ullman
papers.summary: When people imagine a scene, they often leave out basic details like the color of a ball, and this study asked whether that reflects real non-commitment or just the same noticing and recall failures seen in perception. Across three experiments (N=3,895), the details left out of imagination didn't correlate with those missed in briefly shown real images. Imagery also unfolded hierarchically, from core entities and spatial relations to physical properties to surface details like color and texture, and interruptions didn't change that order, supporting a hierarchical partial-scene construction account.
papers.abstract: When calling an image before the mind's eye, people often do not include basic properties of the mental scene. For example, when imagining a person knocking a ball off a table, people may neglect to consider the color of the ball. This "non-commitment" in imagery has been part of ongoing debates on the nature of mental imagery in philosophy and cognitive science, but the central question of its origin remains open. It is possible that this lack of detail in the imagination reflects actual non-commitment, as one constructs a hierarchical mental scene. But it is also possible that people do form highly detailed mental images, but fail to notice, encode, or recall properties of the image, for the same reasons that they do not notice, encode, or recall details of real scenes in direct perception. We tested these contrasting hypotheses across three experiments (N=3,895 total). First, we compared non-commitment patterns in mental imagery with the details that participants failed to notice in briefly presented real images. We found no correlation between properties that were non-committed to in the imagination, and those missed under rapid perception, indicating that non-commitment does not simply arise from perceptual noise. Next, we examined the temporal unfolding of mental imagery, and found consistent evidence of a hierarchical pattern: core entities and spatial relations, then physical properties, then surface details like color and texture. Attempts to interrupt or constrain scene construction did not change the hierarchical ordering. We suggest the results support a hierarchical partial-scene construction account of mental imagery.

papers.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
papers.authors: Troy Houser, Riley Acker, Dagmar Zeithamova
papers.summary: Rodent work suggests the hippocampus cycles between encoding and retrieval at theta rhythm, and here the authors tried to detect that in humans with dense behavioral sampling. They used an attention-grabbing cue to reset theta phase and varied the delay before the to-be-remembered item. Associative memory fluctuated with theta rhythmicity, best fit at 8 Hz, and a second experiment showed memory precision also fluctuated, which fits hippocampal models where processing pathways shift in engagement. It's interesting that this rapid neural rhythm can be seen from behavior alone.
papers.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

papers.title: Diverging Influences of Punishment Motivation and Negative Affect on Cognitive Control
papers.authors: Rachel Elizabeth Brough, Chase Spurbeck, Kimberly Sarah Chiew
papers.summary: Across two experiments using the AX-CPT, a task that measures whether people prepare ahead (proactive control) or react as needed (reactive control), the researchers manipulated negative emotion and the threat of mild electric shocks. Threat of punishment increased proactive control, especially when the shock depended on performance, while uncertainty about punishment had no group-level effect. The takeaway is that any motivator seems to boost proactive control whatever its valence, whereas negative affect itself has a messier relationship that depends on context and individual traits like anxiety.
papers.abstract: The modulation of cognitive control by threat of punishment has been under-characterized relative to examinations of reward, with mixed findings reported in the literature. Across two experiments, we examined the balance of proactive and reactive control in the AX-CPT under several negative affect and punishment manipulations. In Experiment 1, we compared cognitive control performance between two task phases: an Affect phase, in which emotionally evocative images were used to induce either Fear, Anger, or Neutral affect, and a Punishment phase, in which the threat of receiving mild electric shocks was either performance-contingent, or unavoidable. In Experiment 2, we examined cognitive control under punishment that was both unavoidable and uncertain, and whether effects of such punishment varied by individual differences in trait anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty. Across both experiments, we observed that threat of punishment was associated with increased proactive control, and that this effect was heightened when punishment was performance-contingent. In contrast, punishment uncertainty did not appear to modulate cognitive control outcomes at the group level. However, exploratory analyses suggested that punishment uncertainty might interact with individual variability in trait anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, and threat-related physiological arousal responses to shape control outcomes. Together, our findings support an account in which the presence of a motivator, regardless of valence, facilitates increased proactive control. In contrast, the relationship between negative affect and cognitive control outcomes may be more complex, and vary both with contextual factors and individual differences.

papers.title: Gambling for redemption: Consequential inconsistency in dynamic decision making
papers.authors: Jared M Hotaling, Luke Sztajnkrycer
papers.summary: People tend to gamble more after a bad outcome than after a good one, even when the future prospects are identical. Across three experiments, the researchers tested three explanations: the gambler's fallacy, a shifting reference point, and a goal-driven aspiration level. For most people the aspiration-level account fit best, meaning they gamble to redeem themselves and reach a target rather than because they misjudge probabilities or value.
papers.abstract: Planning under uncertainty is vital for effective decision-making, but human planners systematically violate normative models by allowing irrelevant past events to distort future choices—a phenomenon termed consequential inconsistency (CI). Despite evidence of CI, little is known about its underlying cognitive mechanisms. Across three experiments, we documented robust evidence for CI—individuals were more likely to gamble following an unfortunate event than after a fortunate one—despite facing consequentially identical prospects. Using computational modeling to test three competing accounts, we found that for most individuals CI is not primarily a failure of probability perception—as posited by the gambler’s fallacy—or utility calculation—as posited by the reference-point shift model—but rather a goal-driven desire to "gamble for redemption," as formalized by the aspiration-level model. These findings elucidate the psychological processes involved in planning, while also revealing the cognitive underpinnings of individual differences in dynamic decision-making.

papers.title: concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
papers.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki, Yuki Yamada
papers.summary: Participants colored in body maps to show where they feel "future," "long," "more," and "large" (and their opposites). The concepts mostly lit up the head and torso, while "long" was tied to the limbs. When the same method was applied to image-generating AI models, they produced reliable body maps, but these looked quite different from the human ones and from each other. So an AI that handles conceptual opposites well isn't necessarily organizing concepts across the body like people do.
papers.abstract: concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

papers.title: A transdiagnostic computational account linking mental fatigue and cognitive effort
papers.authors: Yang Yang, Akina Umemoto, Senne Braem et al.
papers.summary: In a 75-minute online study with 529 adults spanning a wide range of psychiatric symptoms, people repeatedly chose between resting and doing a hard working-memory task while reporting their fatigue. Fatigue built up over time and predicted avoiding effort. Higher anxious-depression scores went with more initial fatigue, faster buildup, and a steeper drop in high-effort choices, whereas compulsivity and intrusive thoughts went with choosing effort more often but performing worse afterward. Lumping everything into "less willingness to try" misses these separate stages, which might explain why earlier results have been inconsistent.
papers.abstract: Motivational impairments are common to many psychiatric conditions, yet associations between psychiatric symptoms and willingness to exert cognitive effort have been inconsistent. Previous studies have mostly analyzed cognitive effort at the moment when people choose to engage in an effortful task, overlooking fatigue before the choice and how the task is executed after the choice. Here we examined this process during a 75-min online experiment involving 529 adults with psychiatric profiles spanning a broad range of symptoms. Participants repeatedly chose between resting and performing a demanding working-memory task, carried out the selected activity, and reported their fatigue. We derived continuous transdiagnostic symptom dimensions and modeled fatigue, effort selection, and task performance across time. Across participants, fatigue accumulated over time, and higher pre-choice fatigue predicted effort avoidance despite high overall task accuracy. Higher anxious-depression scores were associated with greater initial fatigue, faster fatigue accumulation, and a progressively steeper decline in high-effort choices. By contrast, higher compulsivity/intrusive thought scores were associated with more frequent high-effort choices but lower accuracy after effort was selected. Motivational dysfunction therefore did not reduce to a general reluctance to exert effort, but emerged through distinct alterations in fatigue accumulation, effort selection, and task execution. A dynamic, process-based account that separates these stages may help reconcile inconsistent findings in effort-based mental health research.

papers.title: Explicit knowledge enables allocentric target but not distractor learning
papers.authors: Litian Chen, Freek van Ede, Heleen A Slagter
papers.summary: Earlier work showed that knowing about a target's likely location can produce learning in world-centered (allocentric) coordinates. Here, in six experiments, people searched while moving their bodies and viewpoint, and were told, or not told, about a high-probability distractor location. Even with explicit knowledge, there was no sign of allocentric learning for distractors, though a separate pair of experiments confirmed it works for targets. It suggests that learning what to ignore isn't just the mirror image of learning where to look.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn to attend to and to ignore specific locations based on statistical regularities. Such statistical learning effects may arise through both implicit and explicit mechanisms and may be expressed in egocentric (viewer-centered) or allocentric (world-centered) reference frames. In the absence of explicit knowledge, statistical learning is typically egocentric, but explicit knowledge can promote allocentric target-location learning. Yet, whether explicit knowledge can similarly promote allocentric distractor-location learning remains unclear. Here, we addressed this question across six experiments. Study 1 (Experiments 1-4; n=95) examined whether explicit knowledge can enable allocentric distractor-location learning using an additional-singleton visual-search task in which participants continuously changed their viewpoint following full-body movements. Participants were either informed (explicit) or uninformed (implicit) about a high-probability distractor location, which was defined relative to their perspective (egocentric) or the environment (allocentric). Unlike what has been reported for target regularities, even with explicit knowledge of the regularity, no evidence for allocentric location learning was found for distractor regularities. Study 2 (Experiments 5-6, n=54) confirmed that explicit knowledge can support allocentric target-location learning in our set-up. Together, these findings indicate that explicit knowledge about world-centered spatial regularities can be exploited when it concerns task-relevant but not task-irrelevant information. This dissociation suggests that learning what to ignore is not simply the inverse of learning where to attend, with important implications for theories of statistical learning and attentional control.

papers.title: A Metastudy on Anchoring Effect Moderators
papers.authors: Dan Schley, Evan Weingarten
papers.summary: The researchers ran a preregistered study with nearly 2,000 US adults who answered general-knowledge questions after seeing high or low numeric anchors, while eight proposed moderators were varied together. High anchors pushed estimates up substantially, and the effect was strongest when the anchor clearly applied to the judgment and sat far from people's unanchored beliefs. Debiasing slightly reduced it, cognitive load slightly increased it, and people who felt they knew more were less swayed. Things like directional wording, decimals, small incentives, and page breaks showed little effect.
papers.abstract: Numeric anchors reliably bias estimates, but theories disagree about which conditions make the effect stronger or weaker. Existing moderator evidence is difficult to interpret because moderators in meta-analyses often combine different operationalizations, samples, stimuli, and domains. We conducted a preregistered metastudy of the canonical experimenter-provided high-versus-low anchoring paradigm, testing whether proposed moderators retain leverage when compared under a common task structure. U.S. adults (N = 1,967) answered eight general-knowledge questions in a fractional factorial design that manipulated eight candidate moderators and measured subjective knowledge after each estimate. Responses were standardized within item, and high anchors shifted estimates upward by 0.57 item-level SDs relative to low anchors. Anchors were most influential when they applied to the target judgment and were farther from the center of unanchored beliefs. Debiasing modestly reduced anchoring, cognitive load modestly increased it, and higher post-judgment subjective knowledge was associated with smaller effects. Directional statements, trailing decimals, modest accuracy incentives, and page breaks produced little evidence of moderation. The findings identify which moderators appear stable across meta-analytic and experimental evidence and which require operationalization-level mapping before they can adjudicate among anchoring mechanisms.

papers.title: Meta-learning attentional strategies in multidimensional reinforcement learning
papers.authors: Mina Habibi, Zhang Chen, Miklos Bognar et al.
papers.summary: In a study of 350 people learning rewards for stimuli, one feature (color or pattern) was informative in general but not perfectly so for individual items. When new stimuli appeared, behavior looked the same whether the informative feature stayed or switched, but modeling showed a different strategy. If the feature stayed the same, people kept a hybrid approach, and if it switched, they leaned more on learning about individual objects, and this shift started almost immediately. It suggests people adjust how abstractly they learn based on how reliable they judge the environment to be.
papers.abstract: Reward learning in complex, multidimensional environments requires balancing abstractgeneralisation with stimulus-specific precision. Previous work suggests that humans initiallyrely on feature-based abstraction to support fast generalisation, before shifting toward moreprecise, object-based learning. We asked whether humans also generalise these attentionalstrategies to novel contexts. In a large-scale study (N = 350), participants learned rewardcontingencies in an environment where one feature dimension (colour or pattern) was informativeat a group level but imperfectly predictive at the stimulus level. In a subsequent phase withnovel stimuli, the informative dimension either remained stable (Repeat) or changed (Switch).Behavioural performance was indistinguishable between conditions, yet computational modellingrevealed a divergence in strategy: when the relevant dimension remained stable, participantsmaintained a hybrid approach; when it switched, participants showed a tendency toward objectbasedlearning, reducing reliance on feature-based abstraction. Time-resolved analyses showedthat this reconfiguration began almost immediately upon entering the new context. Humanstherefore tune the level of abstraction they use based on inferred environmental reliability,striking a balance between rapid generalisation and stimulus-specific precision.

papers.title: Control Dilemmas Exist on Different Levels of Information Processing: Flexibility and Stability Trade off at the Task Level
papers.authors: Andrea Janker, Sebastian Musslick, Gesine Dreisbach
papers.summary: Whether flexibility and stability trade off may depend on the level of processing at which you look. In three experiments where people switched between categorization tasks while ignoring distractors, shielding against the other task's distractors worked at the task level. At the stimulus level, learned stimulus-response associations bypassed that shielding. Where shielding operated, it helped when the task repeated but hurt when it switched, which supports a real trade-off at the task level.
papers.abstract: Our cognitive system must manage two opposing demands: staying focused on one task (stability) and switching between tasks when needed (flexibility). Traditionally, a trade-off has been assumed between these two control modes. Recent studies questioned this idea. However, they do not consider that experimental manipulations can influence stability and flexibility at different levels of information processing and that a trade-off may only exist within the same level. We introduce a novel paradigm designed to investigate flexibility and stability at different levels of information processing (task vs. stimulus level). Participants switched between two categorization tasks while ignoring distractors. Distractors either came from the same (within-task) or the alternative task (between-task) and were either response-congruent or incongruent.
