In Experiments 1 and 2, participants categorized words superimposed on distractor images representing the generic response categories (task level interference). In Experiment 3, they categorized letters or digits flanked by distractor letters or digits (stimulus level interference). Reduced interference from between-task distractors compared to within-task distractors in Experiments 1 and 2 show shielding at the task level. At the stimulus level (Experiment 3) both distractor-types interfered to the same extent, indicating that the shielding against between-task distractors got bypassed by the automatic retrieval of learnt stimulus-response associations. Across all three experiments, shielding against between-task distractors in the previous trial improved subsequent performance, when the task repeated (i.e. it improved stability), but impaired performance, when the task switched (i.e. it impaired flexibility). This finding supports a trade-off between flexibility and stability at the task level.

papers.title: Explicit knowledge modulates Pavlovian attentional biases
papers.authors: Francisco Garre-Frutos, Pablo Martínez-López, Adriana Ariza et al.
papers.summary: Stimuli paired with reward can grab attention automatically, even when looking at them costs you the reward. Across three experiments, verbal instructions alone changed these learned attentional biases after the contingencies reversed, and when people weren't told, their biases tracked how aware they were of the new contingencies. Modeling of an earlier dataset suggests instructions trigger a quick revaluation of the stimuli, which can backfire by drawing attention to the previously high-value distractor.
papers.abstract: There is plenty of evidence showing that the history of stimulus-reward pairings can cause such stimuli to capture our attention more easily, even when attending to them actually prevents the delivery of a reward. Once established, these Pavlovian attentional biases are believed to operate automatically and persist even when they no longer predict a reward. This reflects an inflexible form of attentional sign-tracking. In this study, we investigated how reversal learning of Pavlovian attentional biases is affected by explicit knowledge. Across three experiments, we demonstrate that verbal instructions alone can modulate previously learned attentional biases (Experiments 1 and 2a) and that, when not informed of the reversal, participants still exhibit strong associations between Pavlovian attentional biases and individual differences in awareness of the new, reversed contingencies (Experiment 2b). Computational modelling of a previously published dataset reveals that instructions may prompt a rapid model-based revaluation by eliciting the automatic updating of the stimuli's value representation. However, such updating can be counterproductive, as attending to the previously high-value distractor reduces the likelihood of receiving a reward when contingencies are re-evaluated. These findings emphazise the importance of explicit knowledge in the updating process.

papers.title: Memory for US valence without memory for US identity? Decomposing contingency memory in evaluative conditioning with a multinomial modeling approach
papers.authors: Karoline Corinna Bading, Jérémy Béna, Marius Barth et al.
papers.summary: In evaluative conditioning, a neutral item becomes liked or disliked after being paired with a positive or negative stimulus. The researchers built a multinomial processing tree model that separates memory for the item pairing, for the specific stimulus's identity, for its valence, and for guessing. Across three experiments, valence memory was distinct from identity memory and was the only memory component that consistently predicted the conditioning effect, even though identity memory was robust. So remembering whether a paired stimulus was good or bad seems to matter more for attitudes than remembering which one it was.
papers.abstract: Evaluative conditioning (EC) refers to a change in the evaluation of a conditioned stimulus (CS) following its pairing with a positive or negative unconditioned stimulus (US). Theories of EC commonly assume that such effects depend on memory for the CS--US pairings and distinguish between memory for the specific US identity and memory for its valence. However, standard measures of CS--US pairing memory confound these components with each other and with guessing processes, limiting the ability to test whether US valence memory constitutes an independent memory representation and hampering comparisons of the relative predictive roles of US identity and US valence memory for EC effects. We introduce an adapted multinomial processing tree (MPT) model that addresses these limitations by jointly estimating CS recognition, US identity memory, US valence memory independent of identity retrieval, and response biases. Across three experiments using different materials and procedures, the model provided good fits to the data and yielded theoretically interpretable parameter estimates. Crucially, US valence memory emerged as dissociable from US identity memory and as the only memory component consistently associated with individual differences in EC effects. By contrast, US identity memory was robust across conditions but did not predict EC. The present findings support the view that memory for US valence is an independent form of contingency memory and demonstrate the utility of the proposed MPT approach for clarifying the memory processes underlying attitude formation.

papers.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
papers.authors: Sophie Bavard, Andrew McWilliams, Flora Chartier et al.
papers.summary: Using a gamified task, the researchers compared how people form global confidence, their sense of how well they've done over a longer stretch, in memory versus perception. In memory, both local accuracy and trial-by-trial confidence fed into global confidence, while in perception only local confidence predicted it. So the process of judging your overall performance appears to differ by cognitive domain.
papers.abstract: While metacognition - our ability to evaluate our own cognitive processes - has been extensively studied by measuring trial-by-trial self-assessments of task performance (local confidence), real-world decisions often require a broader perspective, drawing on evaluations of performance over wider timespans (global confidence). Despite its pervasive influence on decision-making and mental health, it remains unknown whether global confidence is formed through similar or distinct processes across cognitive domains. Here we employ a novel gamified approach to compare how global confidence is formed in the domains of memory and perception. In memory, we found that both local accuracy and confidence contributed to global confidence, whereas in perception, global confidence was predicted by local confidence alone. By comparing the formation of global confidence across domains, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underpinning self-evaluation, paving the way for the development of metacognitive interventions in education and psychiatry.

papers.title: Context-specific adaptation of cognitive processing in changing virtual environments
papers.authors: Ulrike Senftleben, Daniel Zeidler, Stefan Scherbaum et al.
papers.summary: The context-specific proportion congruency effect is when people adjust how much they handle conflict depending on a cue that predicts it. Here, a numerical Stroop task was run in virtual reality, alternating between a forest and an office, with one mostly congruent and the other mostly incongruent. The usual effect showed up, with a smaller congruency cost in the mostly-incongruent environment. That supports the idea that this kind of learning works in rich, realistic settings and not just with simple 2D cues.
papers.abstract: Human cognition is sensitive to context cues, as indicated by the context-specific proportion congruency (CSPC) effect. This effect demonstrates that individuals implicitly adapt their cognitive processing to contextual cues that predict the likelihood of conflict. However, CSPC paradigms typically rely on simple, two-dimensional context cues, raising questions about their validity for complex, real-life environments. In this preregistered study, we examined whether CSPC effects emerge in three-dimensional, naturalistic contexts delivered via virtual reality (VR). We presented a numerical Stroop task in two virtual environments—a forest and an office—alternating on a trial-by-trial basis. Unbeknownst to participants, each environment was paired with either a high (80%; mostly congruent/MC context) or low (20%; mostly incongruent/MI context) proportion of incongruent trials (counter-balanced). Our results show the typical CSPC effect: reduced response time differences between incongruent and congruent trials in the MI environment relative to the MC environment. This finding indicates that context-dependent adjustments of cognitive processing extend to complex, semantically meaningful virtual environments. This supports the ecological validity of CSPC learning and highlights the importance of context cues in real-life cognitive processing. Further, our study highlights how VR opens up new avenues for studying context-dependent cognition beyond conventional laboratory stimuli.

papers.title: Continuous developmental changes in word recognition support language learning across early childhood
papers.authors: Michael C. Frank, Virginia A. Marchman, Claire Augusta Bergey et al.
papers.summary: Pooling 26 eye-tracking datasets from the Peekbank database, covering over 2,500 children aged 6 months to 6 years, the researchers found that word recognition gets faster, more accurate, and less variable with age, like a gradually learned skill. Speed, accuracy, and vocabulary size covaried, and children who recognized words faster tended to gain vocabulary faster. Growth in recognition skill wasn't specifically tied to vocabulary growth, though, so the two seem intertwined rather than one directly driving the other.
papers.abstract: Being a fluent language user involves recognizing words as they unfold in time. How does this skill develop over the course of early childhood? And how does facility in word recognition relate to the growth of vocabulary knowledge? We address these questions using data from Peekbank, an open database of experiments measuring children's eye movements during early word recognition. In an observational study of 26 datasets from over 2,500 children ages 6 months -- 6 years, we show that word recognition becomes faster, more accurate, and less variable across development, consistent with a process of skill learning. Factor analysis reveals covariation of word recognition speed and accuracy with children's vocabulary size in cross-sectional analysis. Further, across a range of longitudinal models, speed, accuracy, and vocabulary were coupled. Children with overall faster word recognition tended to show faster vocabulary growth, though developmental growth in word recognition skill was not specifically associated with growth in vocabulary. Together, these findings support the view that word recognition is a skill that develops gradually across early childhood and that this skill is deeply intertwined with early language learning.

papers.title: Generalizable experiment agents threaten online behavioral experiments
papers.authors: Talha Özüdoğru, Andrey Chetverikov, Richard Huskey et al.
papers.summary: The researchers built a general-purpose AI agent, using only natural-language prompts and a consumer LLM subscription, that completed 26 online behavioral experiments across seven hosting platforms without task-specific training. On the N-back, Tower of London, and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test it performed within typical human ranges, and it behaved in a human-like way on seven held-out studies. That's a worrying sign for online research, since the assumption that participants are human may not hold, and safeguards will need to keep up.
papers.abstract: Online behavioral experiments rely on the assumption that participants are human. Advances in large language models(LLMs) challenge this assumption, but previous demonstrations have largely focused on surveys or agents built for individualexperimental tasks. Here, we introduce the Artificial General Experiment Agent (AGEA), a general-purpose agent developedentirely through natural language prompting using a consumer-level LLM subscription. Without custom training for anyspecific task, AGEA completed twenty-six online behavioral experiments across seven hosting platforms, independentlyinferring each task’s structure. Benchmark comparisons across three cognitive domains, using the N-back, Tower of London,and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, showed performance within typical human ranges, including changes in accuracy andresponse time with experimental conditions. It further completed, with human-like behavior, seven held-out studies preparedin the spirit of adversarial collaboration between the co-authors. These findings show that agent participation can extendacross experimental paradigms and platforms. As general-purpose agents become cheaper and more capable, they pose agrowing risk to the integrity of online behavioral research, and safeguards must keep pace.

papers.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
papers.authors: Sebastián Mancha, Ellen Lau
papers.summary: Past work suggested people chunk sentences by clause, because recall accuracy shows primacy and recency bumps within each clause. Here the idea is that this pattern may come from nouns, which are remembered better, tending to fall at clause boundaries. In immediate serial recall of two-clause sentences with noun placement manipulated, nouns gave a large accuracy boost at the internal boundary, enough to explain the earlier results. It's a good caution about applying serial-position logic to structured sentences.
papers.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

papers.title: Differential effects of probabilistic retro-cues on search guidance and memory maintenance
papers.authors: Alexandre Fortuna, Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel
papers.summary: Participants did a combined visual search and memory recall task in which a retro-cue (a cue shown after the item to be remembered) pointed to the item that would matter, and the cue was reliable 50, 70, 80 or 100% of the time, or absent. Search got better when reliability rose from 50% to 70% and then leveled off, whereas memory precision improved only when the cue was present and again when it was fully reliable. Neither an all-or-none switch nor a smooth linear shift in priority fits that pattern, which points to flexible prioritization that differs depending on whether the memory is guiding search or being recalled. High reliability also made invalid cues costlier for memory.
papers.abstract: While some debate has recently focused on whether attentional templates are stored in discrete, binary states, a question remains: to what extent can their priority be flexibly adjusted according to probabilistic information and current task demands? We investigated this flexibility by manipulating retro-cue reliability across five conditions (absent, 50%, 70%, 80% and 100%) in a paradigm combining visual search and continuous memory recall. We tested whether priority allocation operates as an all-or-none switch or varies with cue reliability, and whether a common prioritization function governs attentional guidance and memory precision. Unexpectedly, although cue reliability modulated performance in both tasks, the task analyses revealed different nonlinear profiles. Search performance improved when cue reliability increased from 50% to 70%, with no further significant gains at higher reliability levels. Memory precision benefited from cue presence relative to the absent-cue condition and improved further only when the cue became fully reliable. Analyses including invalid trials showed that cue reliability altered the balance between cued and uncued representations, with high reliability increasing the cost of invalid cueing in memory. These findings are not readily explained by either a strictly all-or-none change in template status or a smooth linear increase in priority, and are instead consistent with flexible prioritization. Probabilistic information appears to influence both the benefits of prioritizing the cued representation and the costs of deprioritizing the uncued representation. These effects may differ depending on whether the representation is used to guide visual search or to support memory recall.

papers.title: Load-Dependent Parameter Scaling in Visual Working Memory Models Reveals the Role of Decoding in Retrieval
papers.authors: Hang Qian, Paul Michael Garrett, Yi Liu et al.
papers.summary: Using simulated data from a population-coding model where more items in memory means fewer neurons per item, the researchers fitted three continuous working memory models and asked which parameter picks up the capacity limit. The answer depended on the decoder: with maximum-likelihood decoding the change showed up in dispersion, while with maximum-output decoding it showed up in amplitude. In real data from a color and orientation reproduction task, amplitude scaling with set size was favored for both features. The takeaway is that fitted parameters partly reflect assumptions about decoding, so they shouldn't be read as straightforward measures of precision or signal strength.
papers.abstract: We examined how recent models of continuous visual working memory (VWM) retrieval express capacity limitations through fitted parameters, and whether these expressions follow the inverse square-root scaling predicted by the sample-size model. Through simulations, we generated response errors from a Poisson population-coding model in which increased memory load was implemented as reduced neural population size per item. We then fitted three continuous VWM models that differed in their noise assumptions and decision rules, comparing model-variants in which load affected either representational dispersion or signal amplitude. The parameter that captured capacity-related change depended systematically on the decoder used to transform population activity into a response estimate. Under maximum-likelihood decoding, reduced population size was expressed primarily through changes in dispersion. Under maximum-output decoding, the same manipulation was expressed primarily through changes in amplitude. We then applied the same model-comparison logic to empirical data from a post-cue continuous memory-reproduction task, in which participants reported either color or orientation of a stimulus after encoding both features. Although the two feature domains produced markedly different error distributions, they both favored scaling of the amplitude parameter with set size. These findings show that parameters in continuous VWM models do not merely summarize response-error distributions; they also reflect assumptions about how population-level representations are decoded into behavior. Set-size related parameter changes should therefore be interpreted with consideration of the assumed decoding process, rather than as decoder-independent measures of memory precision or signal strength.

papers.title: Why do preschoolers struggle with the 3-cups-task? Further evidence for cognitive asymmetries in representing what and where uncertainty
papers.authors: Marlene M. Meyer, Marina Proft, Hannes Rakoczy
papers.summary: Three-year-olds can acknowledge uncertainty about which of two objects is in a box, yet they stumble on the 3-cups task, where they should prefer a sure reward over two uncertain cups. Across three preregistered experiments with 278 children, the team found little evidence that task pragmatics or question format explained the difficulty. What mattered was the content of the uncertainty: children found it much harder to represent uncertainty about where an object is than about which object it is. This suggests a where/what asymmetry in early reasoning about possibilities, and raises questions about how solid early modal competence really is.
papers.abstract: Prior research on modal thought has yielded conflicting findings regarding children’s ability to represent mutually exclusive possibilities. While some studies suggest that even infants and non-human animals understand possibilities to some degree, older children struggle in experimental paradigms that require them to consider multiple alternatives. In the 3-cups-task, for instance, they fail to systematically prefer a certain reward (in A) over two uncertain options (in B or C). This has been taken as evidence for that children below age 4 lack genuinely modal representations of possibility. However, recent metacognitive research suggests that already three-year-old children can recognize epistemic uncertainty about possible, mutually exclusive object identities (X or Y). So, why do 3-year-olds metacognitively acknowledge their ignorance in some contexts, but obviously fail to do so in trying to solve the 3-cups task? We addressed this question in three preregistered experiments (N = 278 three-year-old children) in which we investigated whether details of the task pragmatics, question format or the contents of the uncertainty judgments pose specific performance factors in the 3-cups-task. There was no clear evidence that task pragmatics or question format per se explain these difficulties. But there was strong evidence that the content of the uncertainty judgments matters: Children found it much more difficult to represent uncertainty where an object is (in cups B or C) than to represent uncertainty which of two objects (X or Y) was in a given box. These results converge with other recent findings to suggest a fundamental where/what asymmetry in children’s early modal reasoning and raise crucial questions about the robustness of early modal competence.

papers.title: Imagination boosts strategy learning
papers.authors: Jack Burgess, Timothy D. Verstynen
papers.summary: A stumbler-strategist reinforcement learning model was used to test whether imagining unplayed scenarios helps learn the optimal strategy in a combinatorial game better than replaying past games. In the model, imagination did boost strategy learning over memory replay. The team then tested this with 255 people who either imagined unplayed scenarios, reviewed prior games, or did a simple visual attention task, and the human results matched the model's prediction.
papers.abstract: Imagination is thought to boost exploration and problem solving by simulating states that have not been directly experienced as a means of reasoning through future plans. Here we tested this idea in the context of an impartial combinatorial game with a ground truth optional strategy. Adopting a stumbler-strategist reinforcement learning architecture, we showed how imagination can boost optimal strategy learning over memory replay. These model predictions were validated experimentally in humans (N=255) using an intervention design where participants were tasked with either imagining unplayed scenarios, reviewing prior games, or engaging in a simple visual attention task (control). These convergent results show how imagination uniquely boosts strategy learning in partially explored tasks.

papers.title: Key Moments and Event Boundaries in Film Comprehension and Memory
papers.authors: Aditya Upadhyayula, Zachariah Reagh, Jeffrey M. Zacks
papers.summary: Event boundaries (where one event ends and another begins) and key moments (especially important points in a story) have been measured in different ways, in real time versus after the fact, which muddles the comparison. Here, participants watched clips from Sherlock and marked either boundaries or key moments, either live with a button press or afterward on a timeline, with everyone assigned to just one combination. Key moments resembled other key moments more than boundaries, and vice versa, so the two constructs partly differ. But the method mattered a lot too: retrospective judgments of the same thing differed from real-time ones, so what people see as event structure depends both on what they look for and when they judge.
papers.abstract: Not all moments we experience carry equal weight. The boundaries between meaningful events (Event Boundaries; EBs) have been found to be important for comprehension and memory. Recently, it has been shown that people can reliably identify Key Moments (KMs) that are somewhat distinct from EBs and play a unique role in both comprehension and memory. Some but not all KMs are EBs, and vice versa. Both EBs and KMs are identified in terms of subjective judgments. However, thus far they have been measured using different psychophysical procedures: EBs have usually been measured concurrently with movie viewing, whereas KMs have been measured retrospectively. This difference confounds the underlying cognitive construct with the psychophysical task. Here we dissociated the subjective construct measured from the psychophysical task. Participants watched clips from the television series Sherlock, and were asked to identify either EBs or KMs, and were asked to do so either by pressing a button in real time while watching or retrospectively using a timeline interface, in a fully crossed between-participants design. The timepoints selected were compared within and across groups. Within both Realtime and Retrospective task paradigms, KM distributions were more similar to other KMs than to EBs and vice-versa, suggesting a partial dissociation between the two constructs. A large and significant effect of the paradigm was also observed: Retrospective estimates of the same construct differed from its Realtime counterparts. These findings demonstrate that people see different structure in events, depending both on whether they are looking for key moments or boundaries and whether they are monitoring the moment or looking back. These variations in the structure are cognitively significant, and important for researchers studying event comprehension.

papers.title: Perceptual load influences the effect of a peripheral visual priming stimulus in a go/no-go task
papers.authors: Fabrício Bacchini Dias, Luiz Eduardo Ribeiro do Valle
papers.summary: A flash at the edge of vision usually speeds responses to a target in the same spot and slows them for one on the opposite side, but earlier work found this effect vanished in a go/no-go task when the go target was a horizontal line and the distractor a vertical one. Three experiments tested why. The earlier result replicated; with no distractor the effect appeared for horizontal targets, and it also came back when the vertical distractor was dimmed. The authors suggest that under high perceptual load, the prime gets less central processing, which is why the attentional effect disappears.
papers.abstract: Several studies have shown that a peripheral visual priming stimulus reduces reaction time to a visual target stimulus at the same position and increases reaction time to a visual target stimulus at the opposite-side position. These effects are commonly attributed to the automatic capture of attention by the prime. However, the size and even the presence of these effects vary according to the exact stimulus conditions and the nature of the task being performed. A previous study from this laboratory, testing volunteers in a go/no-go task, demonstrated that the attentional effect, defined as the difference between reaction time to the target at the opposite-side position and reaction time to the target at the same position, occurred when the go target was a vertical line and the contralateral distracting stimulus was a horizontal line, but not when the go target was the horizontal line and the distractor was the vertical line. The present study investigated whether this second finding was related to selective forward masking of the horizontal line by the prime, to the high salience of the vertical line as distractor, or to a decrease in the central processing of the prime possibly related to the high perceptual load of the task. Three experiments using a go/no-go task were performed. Experiment 1 replicated the previous study with a larger number of volunteers and obtained the same pattern of results. In Experiment 2, no distractor was presented, and a clear-cut attentional effect was observed for the horizontal line as go target. In Experiment 3, the vertical distractor was reintroduced with lower luminance, to decrease its perceptual salience, and the attentional effect again appeared for the horizontal line as go target. The results suggest that the absence of the attentional effect under high perceptual load may be related to reduced central processing of the prime.

papers.title: Preschoolers can coordinate with each other to communicate about novel referents
papers.authors: Veronica Boyce, Robert Zane Sparks, Michael C. Frank
papers.summary: Earlier iterated reference games suggested that 4-5-year-olds struggle to agree on names for novel things. Here, pairs of children played a simpler, child-friendly version, and across four experiments with 82 pairs (158 kids) they managed to establish reference with each other, reaching 81% accuracy and often echoing their partner's descriptions. So the ability to build effective referring expressions in new situations seems to show up earlier than previously thought, at least when the setting is supportive.
papers.abstract: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring sustained interactive communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4-5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children's referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 4 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N=158), we found that 4-5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner's. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

papers.title: The Limits of Identifiability in the Self-Exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Model
papers.authors: Hannah Pongratz, Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
papers.summary: One recent account of speed-accuracy tradeoffs says that rushing induces a confirmation bias toward the currently favored option, which can be modeled with a self-exciting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Using asymptotic arguments and extensive simulations, the researchers show that under certain conditions the model's key parameters can't be jointly identified, meaning different combinations fit equally well. They explain why this happens, discuss what it means for model-based inference, and suggest ways to resolve or lessen the problem.
papers.abstract: Evidence-accumulation models play a central role in the field of decision-making research, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding choice behavior and response times, including speed–accuracy tradeoffs (SATs). In this framework, the dominant explanation for SATs has long been that prioritizing speed lowers the boundary separation, meaning less evidence is needed to make a choice. Recently, however, an alternative account has been proposed according to which emphasizing speed induces a confirmation bias toward the currently favored option. Such a behavior can be formally captured by a self-exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. However, drawing on asymptotic arguments and extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, key parameters of the resulting evidence-accumulation model are not jointly identifiable. We explain the underlying cause of this identifiability issue, examine its practical consequences for model-based inference, andpresent potential strategies to resolve or mitigate it.

papers.title: Patterns of belief perseverance and polarization reflect a resource-rational balance of epistemic and instrumental utilities
papers.authors: Rebekah A. Gelpí, Pablo Leon-Villagra, William A. Cunningham et al.
papers.summary: Belief polarization has been explained by differing priors, accuracy-versus-effort tradeoffs, and motivated reasoning. Here, a resource-limited particle filter, which approximates Bayesian updating with a small set of hypotheses that get resampled and refreshed, is combined with a term for the instrumental value of holding a belief. Tested against four earlier polarization studies, models with few particles and limited rejuvenation matched human behavior best. Group-level polarization came out more conservative than normative models predict, even though many individuals overreacted to evidence compared with an ideal Bayesian. Polarization and belief perseverance can thus look like rational compromises under limited computational resources.
papers.abstract: Belief polarization—the divergence of two individuals' beliefs despite encountering the same information—has been proposed to result from various mechanisms, including differing prior beliefs, trade-offs between accuracy and cognitive cost, and deviations from rationality due to motivated cognition. We propose a unified, resource-rational account of belief perseverance and polarization in which agents approximate Bayesian updating with a resource-limited particle filter model that adaptively resamples and rejuvenates a set of hypotheses upon observing evidence. By balancing epistemic objectives with the instrumental utility of holding a belief, the framework additionally captures the potential influences of motivated reasoning. We evaluate a family of resource-rational and motivated reasoning models on four past studies in which individuals exhibit belief polarization. Across studies, we find that models with modest particle counts and limited rejuvenation best reproduce human behaviour on the tasks; interestingly, this leads to polarization that is often more conservative at the group level than the predictions of normative models, despite the fact that a large proportion of individuals overreacts to the evidence relative to an ideal Bayesian observer. These results demonstrate that patterns of belief perseverance and polarization can be understood as rational compromises between epistemic accuracy and instrumental goals under bounded computational resources, offering a parsimonious mechanistic account of divergent belief updating across diverse domains.

papers.title: Explaining Brain Computation Through Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Martina Gonzalez Vilas, Federico G Adolfi, Bhavin Choksi et al.
papers.summary: This is a conceptual proposal for using mechanistic interpretability, a set of tools for working out what computations are going on inside deep networks, to link DNNs to the brain. One route extracts mechanisms from models and turns them into hypotheses about neural implementation, while the other starts from observed brain-model matches and looks for the model components that could explain them. The two routes constrain each other and are refined iteratively when models and data disagree. The aim is to treat DNNs as 'model organisms' for studying the brain's algorithms.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly used to model brain computation, yet the principles linking their internal operations to neural mechanisms remain elusive. We propose a framework which leverages a recent advance in the interpretability of DNNs---mechanistic interpretability---to uncover shared algorithmic structure between DNNs and the brain via two parallel pathways. The Mechanism-to-Brain pathway uses interpretability to extract computational mechanisms from models that generate hypotheses about neural implementation. The Brain-to-Mechanism pathway begins from observed brain–model correspondences and applies interpretability to identify model components that could instantiate similar computations. These pathways interact through mutual constraints, ensuring that advances in one domain inform and delimit inquiry in the other, and through iterative refinement, where discrepancies between models and data drive the reciprocal revision of both mechanistic analyses and neuroscientific hypotheses. Together, they establish a principled route toward causal, mechanistic explanations of cognition, positioning DNNs as computational model organisms for probing the algorithms of the brain.

papers.title: Using biologically inspired visual statistics to predict texture memorability
papers.authors: Federico De Filippi, Olivier Penacchio, Akira O'Connor et al.
papers.summary: Can purely visual features, not meaning, make an image memorable? The researchers used a model of early vision, with orientation- and scale-tuned receptive fields plus color-opponency, to pick textures that should produce high or low visual stimulation, and 100 observers rated how memorable each looked and then did a recognition test. Textures that drove stronger model activity were rated more memorable and recognized better. Pattern and color contrast statistics explained a lot of the variance in memorability ratings but much less in actual recognition, so early visual signals seem to shape our sense of memorability more than memory itself.
papers.abstract: We might remember an image for its meaning, but purely visual features may also contribute. Although some image properties that increase visual stimulation (such as size and contrast) are known to enhance memory, the role of an image's local spatial structure remains unclear. We used a computational model of early vision to test whether the patterns of activity evoked by a texture predict how well human observers remember it. Orientation- and spatial-scale-selective receptive fields were combined with colour-opponency mechanisms to quantify population luminance and colour processing of a large set of texture images with minimal semantic content. We used the model to select stimuli that offered either high or low visual stimulation. One hundred observers rated how 'memorable' each image appeared (metamemory rating), then completed a memory test distinguishing previously seen images from novel ones (recognition). Textures evoking stronger activity were associated with higher metamemory ratings and enhanced recognition performance. However, while pattern and colour contrast statistics explained a large proportion of the variance in metamemory ratings (suggesting an influence of early visual processing), they explained less variance in recognition performance, indicating a smaller influence on recognition. These findings highlight which visual signals are likely to influence memory (and our perception of it) within a neurobiologically plausible feature space.

papers.title: Developmental differences in probabilistic reinforcement learning reflect strategy engagement rather than parameter changes
papers.authors: Kristina Pultsina, Galina Kozunova, Boris Chernyshev et al.
papers.summary: Adolescents' poorer performance in probabilistic learning has often been blamed on more exploration and overestimating volatility, but those accounts assume everyone uses the same model-based strategy. Here, 36 adolescents and 67 adults did a probabilistic learning task, and each person's behavior was fit with a random baseline, a win-stay/lose-shift heuristic, or a hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning model. Model-based behavior showed up in only some adolescents but dominated in adults, and people classified as model-based had similar parameters across ages. The age difference thus appears to reflect how often the model-based strategy is engaged rather than different underlying parameters, and model-based adolescents had higher IQ.
papers.abstract: Theoretical accounts of decision-making distinguish between two reinforcement-learning strategies: a model-based system that supports goal-directed choices through internal representations of action–outcome contingencies, and a model-free system that updates action values based on recent rewards, often approximating a win–stay/lose–shift (WSLS) pattern. While previous studies have characterized these mechanisms, their developmental trajectory remains unclear. Prevailing accounts attribute adolescents’ poorer performance in probabilistic learning to increased exploration and overestimation of environmental volatility, based on Bayesian models assuming a shared model-based strategy across age groups but differing latent parameters. Such approaches may overlook model-free contributions and individual variability, particularly during adolescence. Here, 36 adolescents and 67 adults completed a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task with binary choices and asymmetric reward contingencies (70:30), presented in sequential blocks to dissociate learning strategies. Individual behavior was fit with competing models: (I) a random baseline, (II) a WSLS heuristic, and (III) a hierarchical reinforcement-learning model implementing Bayesian adaptive learning. The results showed that both strategies contributed to behavior in each group, but in different proportions: model-based strategy was evident in only a subset of adolescents and became predominant in adults. Critically, individuals classified as model-based showed comparable latent parameters (e.g., learning rate, model strength, inverse temperature, precision) across age groups, and WSLS behavior also did not differ between adolescents and adults. Adolescents exhibiting model-based behavior had higher IQ but did not differ in age from their peers. Our findings indicate that in stable probabilistic environments, developmental differences in decision-making between adolescents and adults reflect variability in the engagement of model-based versus model-free strategies rather than differences in underlying computational parameters, with both groups behaving similarly when using the same strategy.

papers.title: Effects of Action Type on the Attentional Boost Effect
papers.authors: Xiangyu Li, Kanji Tanaka
papers.summary: The attentional boost effect is the memory advantage for images shown at the same time as a detected target, and it reliably appears with simple button presses. Across three experiments, people did a Go/No-go task while encoding background images, responding either with a key press or a swipe in a cued direction. When targets could appear at eight locations, the effect showed up for taps but not swipes, but with targets at the screen center it appeared for both. So more demanding actions don't weaken the effect on their own; instead, the visuospatial attention tied to the action setup may modulate its size.
papers.abstract: The attentional boost effect (ABE) refers to the enhancement of memory for concurrently presented information when a target is detected during a dual task. Although ABE reliably emerges with simple motor responses, such as button presses (i.e., taps), it remains unclear whether it generalizes to actions with higher cognitive demands, such as swipe actions. The present study investigated how action type (tap vs. swipe) and the visuospatial attention associated with each action task influence the ABE. Across three experiments, participants performed a Go/No-go task while encoding background images, followed by a recognition test. In the tap condition, participants pressed a key in response to Go cues, whereas in the swipe condition, they swiped in the direction indicated by the target. In Experiment 1, potential targets appeared at eight spatially distributed locations. The Result showed that the ABE emerged in the tap condition but not in the swipe condition. In Experiments 2 and 3, targets were presented at the center of the screen, and ABEs were observed for both actions. Reaction times were consistently shorter for taps than for swipes. These findings suggest that action-related cognitive demands do not attenuate the ABE; rather, visuospatial attention linked to specific action environments may modulate its magnitude.

papers.title: Amortized Bayesian Workflow for Modeling Congruency Effects Using the Diffusion Model for Conflict Tasks
papers.authors: Simon B. Schaefer, Stefan T. Radev, Jan Göttmann et al.
papers.summary: Fitting the Diffusion Model for Conflict Tasks, which captures congruency effects in tasks like the flanker, is computationally slow with standard methods. The researchers used amortized Bayesian inference, a deep-learning approach where a network is trained once and then gives fast posterior estimates, within a structured workflow. It produced well-calibrated estimates as accurate as iterative methods at a fraction of the runtime. In a flanker experiment varying stimulus spacing, the automatic-process amplitude responded as expected, but the peak latency effect depended on the parameterization and priors chosen.
papers.abstract: The congruency effect, characterized by faster and more accurate performance in congruent compared to incongruent trials, has been consistently observed in various conflict tasks. However, the search for common underlying attentional control processes reveals significant differences between conflict tasks, as evident from different time courses of the congruency effect (i.e., delta functions) and a lack of correlations in performance across different conflict tasks. To address these issues, the Diffusion Model for Conflict Tasks (DMC) has been employed to explicitly model congruency effects and explain different delta function shapes. However, estimating the parameters of the DMC using standard iterative methods faces computational challenges. In this study, we leverage Amortized Bayesian Inference (ABI) with deep learning to address these limitations. We use different prior distributions, levels of model complexity, and automated hyperparameter optimization within a principled workflow. ABI produces well-calibrated posteriors across a wide range of trial counts, estimating individual-level parameters as accurately as iterative methods, while requiring only a fraction of their runtime once the initial training phase is complete. Additionally, we selectively manipulated irrelevant information strength in a flanker task to assess the sensitivity of DMC parameters to experimental effects. As expected, the amplitude of the automatic process was influenced by stimulus spacing in a flanker paradigm. However, the effect on the peak latency parameter depended on the choice of model parameterization and prior hyperparameters. Taken together, we demonstrate the viability of ABI as a scalable, accurate alternative to conventional estimation techniques and provide a reproducible workflow for future cognitive modeling studies.

papers.title: Intrusive and voluntary memory from a single system: A retrieved-context account of selective interference in the trauma-film paradigm
papers.authors: Jordan Gunn, Richard Henson, Emily A Holmes et al.
papers.summary: Studies with distressing films show that a reminder followed by a task like Tetris can cut later intrusive memories while leaving deliberate memory mostly intact, which is often taken to mean two separate memory systems. Here, an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval model gives a single-system alternative: imagery during the task becomes linked to the film's context and competes with film memories at retrieval. For deliberate recall, the model assumes people maintain a retrieval cue distinguishing film from task material. Simulations reproduced the selective-interference pattern only when that cue was sustained, suggesting competitor learning and cueing within one memory system can be enough.
papers.abstract: Memory theory must explain why interference can affect deliberate and involuntary remembering differently. Studies using distressing films show that a film reminder followed by an imagery-competing task such as Tetris can reduce later spontaneous memories of the film (intrusions) while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact. This selective interference effect is often interpreted through clinical theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and voluntary remembering depend on different memory representations. We develop an alternative account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events. Events become associated with context, a changing internal representation of experience. A film reminder reinstates film-associated context, so mental imagery generated during the subsequent task becomes associated with that context. During later retrieval, task memories compete with film memories cued by the same context, reducing film recall without weakening the original film associations. During deliberate recall, however, we propose that people pursue the goal of remembering the film by constructing and maintaining a retrieval cue that distinguishes film from task material. In simulations, sustained support from this cue was required to reproduce the selective-interference pattern across reminder and task conditions, protecting deliberate recall relative to involuntary retrieval. These results suggest that competitor learning and retrieval cueing can produce selective interference within a shared memory system, motivating tests in other memory tasks.
